prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that made incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The argument is that this is a specific discovery with a discernible change in the field. Holst's human physiology of GLP-1 secretion and action, Drucker's biology of GLP-1 and GLP-2 and the therapeutic rationale, and Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide together define the incretin mechanism. That mechanism is now confirmed over two decades by independent outcome trials in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal disease. The arc from hormone physiology to medicine is complete and unusually clear, and I do not think waiting longer adds anything. A single-achievement prize also keeps the citation clean and avoids forcing a second part that would squeeze the credited names.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the weak point. Choosing Mojsov over Knudsen, or Knudsen over Mojsov, is a judgement about whether the prize rewards the identification of the active peptide or the long-acting analogues that became the dominant drugs. Habener and others who worked on proglucagon-derived peptides are outside the supplied credit list, and Mojsov's priority is disputed. A prize built on contested priority would be criticised whichever way we go. There is also a reasonable view that the pharmaceutical development belongs to industry and that the physiology alone was already honoured by earlier prizes, while the true clinical breakthrough rests on drug engineering the committee cannot credit without exceeding three names.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, on the view that long-acting analogue design leading to liraglutide and semaglutide is the translational step that produced the therapies.
responses.response: I take the argument seriously, but I do not agree. The prize recognises a discovery, and Knudsen's work is a drug-development achievement within a company, built on peptide and physiology knowledge that others established. Mojsov's identification of the active truncated peptide is part of that foundation. I would only move toward Knudsen if the supplied evidence showed that Mojsov's contribution was derivative or not independent. As it stands, I still think Mojsov has the stronger claim to the third place. This is a real disagreement about what the prize rewards, and I do not think it needs to be resolved by compromise.

responses.point: El-Manira ranked GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, but said Mojsov's priority is contested and that he is working from recollection rather than verified evidence.
responses.response: I share the doubt about priority and I agree it is the main open issue. I would add that a contested priority claim is not the same as a weak scientific contribution. The identification and synthesis of GLP-1(7-36) was necessary for everything that followed, and the disagreement is mostly about who credit should go to within one laboratory network, with Habener also relevant. We should ask for the documentary record before a final vote instead of settling this from memory. If the record is genuinely unclear, the cleaner fallback is a two-name GLP-1 prize, not an unsupported third name.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranked optogenetics second and TNF blockade fourth, describing optogenetics as a general method of exceptional breadth, and favoured a Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth configuration.
responses.response: Optogenetics is the strongest of the alternatives on impact, and I ranked it fourth only because of attribution. Six credited names, with Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck all having strong claims, cannot be reduced to three without excluding someone whom the field regards as essential. That is a problem of credit, not of merit. I would put the unfolded protein response second for that reason, since Walter and Mori are a clean pair. I do not think optogenetics should be held back, but it will be hard to fit within three names, and a tool prize also has to show change in understanding, not only in experimental practice.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked CAR-T second and TNF blockade third, stressing durable clinical remissions and a new class of living therapy, and noting extension into autoimmune disease.
responses.response: The clinical impact of CAR-T cells is not in doubt, but I place it below the others for two reasons. First, Eshhar's foundational chimeric receptor work is not in the credited names, so the trio of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg is not a clean reflection of the discovery. Second, solid-tumour results and long-term safety are still unsettled, and the autoimmune extension is early. I would be more persuaded if the committee could define a single discovery for the citation. TNF blockade is mature and compact, but I see it as a therapeutic proof of concept in which the mechanistic discovery was made by others outside the supplied credit.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen deserves the third GLP-1 credit, and how Habener's work and Mojsov's disputed priority should be weighed given the supplied credit list.
Whether a two-name GLP-1 prize (Drucker and Holst) is a better fallback if the documentary evidence on the peptide identification is unclear.
Whether optogenetics can be reduced to three names without excluding a co-discoverer, which determines how strongly it competes with the unfolded protein response as a second option.
I have relied on my recollection and the supplied ballots, not on documents, for several of the attribution details.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented work on nuclear receptors and dopamine neurons does not overlap with any shortlisted ballot. My profile notes about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson and one with Abdel El Manira, but these do not concern any shortlisted candidate. I also note that the profile does not establish the voting status of the Secretary-General.
